messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Patel had grown up in a small apartment in Queens with the sounds of his parents’ marriage leaking through the walls, but one night in particular had never loosened its grip on him. He was nine when he heard his mother crying in the kitchen and found his father shoving her against the counter, a lamp falling and shattering beside them. Arjun remembered freezing in the doorway, his chest tight, unable to make sense of the scene except that it felt like terror itself had entered the room. Even now, he could not put the event into words without stalling; it remained less a story than a rush of bodily fear and fragments — the crash of glass, his mother’s sobbing, his own small hands gripping the frame. When that memory returned, it brought back the same terror he had felt then, and he hated how suddenly it could happen, as if something in the world could open the whole scene without warning.

In the years after, Arjun came to believe that the men who hurt women like that never truly paid for it. His father had faced no consequences that mattered to him as a child, and that belief settled into a bitter conviction that bad things happened and no one stopped them. He also grieved a version of himself he felt he had lost; he used to think of himself as easygoing and even cheerful, but after the divorce and the years of strain that followed, he described himself as almost always miserable, as though the life he had wanted had been taken and never given back. He was certain that he could not stop bad things from happening to him or to the people he cared about, and that helplessness sat underneath nearly everything he did. When he recalled the old violence, the memory did not stay contained; it immediately fed his sense that the world was unfair and ungoverned, which in turn made the fear feel more urgent and more unavoidable.

Arjun worked as an accountant in a downtown office, where the silence of the rows of computers and the sudden clang of a filing cabinet could jolt him far more than he wanted anyone to know. A colleague dropping a heavy binder, a door slamming in the hallway, or even a sharp argument in the break room could bring the whole scene back in a flash. In those moments his body reacted before he could think: his heart raced, his shoulders locked, his stomach clenched, and he felt keyed up as if something dangerous were about to break into the office. He stayed superalert at work and in public, watching doorways, scanning voices, and sitting where he could see exits. The more his body stayed on guard, the more the memory seemed to rush in uninvited; when his muscles tensed and his pulse jumped, the old kitchen scene became easier to summon, as though his own alarm system were calling it up. That same flood of remembered terror then deepened what he already believed — that no one had protected his mother, that no one would intervene now, and that he remained powerless — and he would leave the office unsettled, carrying the conviction that danger could arrive at any moment.

Over time Arjun began arranging his life around the possibility of being caught off guard. He avoided family gatherings where loud voices might rise, and he kept his apartment television low because shouting from a show could set off the same physical surge. At work he volunteered less and lingered after meetings so he would not have to pass through crowded hallways when people were irritated or hurried. His divorce had narrowed his daily world further; he said he no longer had the energy to be the man he had once imagined being, and he often withdrew rather than risk being exposed as tense or afraid. Yet the withdrawal only gave his mind more room to replay what had happened and to return to the same bleak conclusions. As the memories came back, so did the bodily alarm, and as the alarm stayed high, the old conviction hardened that harm was always just outside the frame. By the time he sought help, Arjun was exhausted by living as if he were always bracing for the next blow. What brought him in was a recent incident at the office when a coworker raised his voice in a tense meeting and Arjun felt his chest seize so sharply he had to step into the stairwell to breathe. He was most afraid that he would remain trapped in this state forever, and most hoping that treatment might help him feel safe enough to stop living as though danger were already in the room.
